story_text.value:
introducing https://call4.me, an ai agent that handles phone calls for you.

you can use it to cancel subscriptions, book medical appointments, dinners, change flights, or anything else possible with a call.

most importantly, it works in claude code & codex. i spend most of my time in the terminal, so i want my productivity tools to live there as well. switching to imessage or another app annoys me.

i've now handled dozens of tasks over the phone using it & am in love. if you're like me & hate breaking concentration to dial, you'll likely love it as well.

it's fully open source: https://github.com/skeptrunedev/call4me

story_text.value:
Switched to Fedora a year ago. And because I needed to transcribe interviews offline from time to time, I was looking for something like MacWhisper for Linux. When I couldn't find one, I decided to build one. Because in this day and age, why the hell not! And yes, AI coding-agents were used.

I work as a .NET Software Engineer and I despise Electron Apps, so I decided to go with a semi-native Stack, consisting of C# and Avalonia.Net (hardware accelerated trough SkiaSharp) for the frontend and C++ for low-level model bindings (CTranslate2 for translation, Nemotron 3 NeMo-Speech.cpp for Speaker Identification via JSON-RPC worker).

A friend liked the app and told me to go Freemium, so here we are. Works also on Windows btw.

title.value: Show HN: TrueScribe – Linux local AI transcription studio

story_text.value:
New benchmark from researchers at Meta, Stanford, Harvard, UW, including the researchers who've worked on SWE-bench, ProgramBench etc.

Most benchmarks just test if AI can fix a problem you've already pointed out.

But obviously it would be much better to fix problems before you or any user runs into it. Like, isn't it crazy that we still have to wait for people to open tickets before a lot of obvious bugs get found?

We wanted to test that capability at scale. Turns out that models still are terrible at it (best setup we tested still fixed < 5% of bugs)

We have 100 repos of 22 languages and 4k bugs between. All the bugs are real-world bugs from github. We do a lot of filtering to ensure everything can be solved in this setting.

===========================================

Sol 5.6 (xhigh) 4.7% $7,230

Luna 5.6 (xhigh) 2.5% $224

Terra 5.6 (xhigh) 1.5% $357

Luna 5.6 (high) 1.4% $28

Opus 5 (xhigh) 1.3% $5,363

Kimi K3 0.6% $2,451

Luna 5.6 0.5% $4

GPT-5.4 Mini (high) 0.5% $122

GPT-5.4 Mini 0.2% $5

Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite 0.1% $6

===========================================

Also the best model is very expensive.

We have a lot more FAQ on the website https://swesweep.com/ Oh and we're all open-source (MIT license) at https://github.com/facebookresearch/swe-sweep

Curious what you all think!

title.value: Show HN: Benchmark: AI doesn't find bugs unless you tell it what's wrong

story_text.value:
I made a way to (sort of) read the Odyssey in Greek without all those years of learning Greek first.

I’ve had a deep interest in reading great literature in its original language since I studied Latin in High School, but wanted to find ways of reading real literature quickly. I’ve used this method myself to read books in several languages including Italian, German, Chinese, Japanese, and Greek. You still have to do the grammar and vocabulary study over time to really comprehend it, but this method has worked far better than all my previous attempts. The goal is to eventually be able just to read the language without any aids, but do that while reading real stuff the entire time. I’ve found that I go from needing help on everything, to learning individual words, to phrases, and then gradually I get to understanding whole sentences without looking anything up. Using a translation helps to keep me honest.

I made a little demo of some lines from the Odyssey Book 1 to share the method and see if other people might find it useful. This is a special version that has a lot of explanation to see if something as difficult as Homeric Greek can be approached from 0. The interlinear translation and notes are AI generated though I made sure to ground them in real translations and existing grammatical tags. The commentary won't be as good as an actual Classical scholar's work and can be overly simplistic, but I'm hoping it's enough to get started. There are other versions that feature progressive grammar learning and identification as well as flashcards. If people are interested I'm happy to share the rest of the book or other texts I've made and read myself. I have the New Testament in Greek and then a bunch of other works in lots of ancient and modern languages.

title.value: Show HN: Read the Odyssey in Greek while learning Greek

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

Some friends and I built an app called Sidekick that joins your telehealth visits in real-time. It explains medical terms and suggests useful questions, including ones you may not have thought to ask. After the visit, it provides a summary including next steps, so you can focus on the conversation instead of taking notes.

The idea of Sidekick came from our team's experiences with healthcare. Our founder, Rahul, had stage three cancer at 17. His mom had to manage everything around his care: taking notes through treatment, figuring out what questions to ask, etc. A decade later and he’s now in remission, but still sees a lot of specialists and deals with the same challenges.

Another teammate became a caregiver after his dad had a severe stroke. He found himself taking notes, looking up medical terms, and trying to keep track of what was said during every doctor visit. Others have dealt with situations like this when navigating pancreatitis and other serious health issues.

These experiences got us interested in how we might be able to reduce the burden on the patient or caregiver.

A lot of products focus on simply recording or summarizing the visit. That's useful and a step in the right direction, but we kept coming back to the fact that a lot of the challenge originates while the conversation is still happening. If you can catch something in the moment, you can address it with your clinician immediately and potentially lead to better outcomes. If you realize you missed something after the visit, then you have to try to get another appointment (and in SF I often can't get another doctor visit till 2 months later).

So we built Sidekick, to help patients and caregivers during a visit in real-time to translate medical jargon and suggest useful questions, ideally without becoming a distraction.

If you want to try it, you can download it on our website. Sidekick is desktop-only for now, but we’re working on a mobile app for in-person visits.

We would be especially interested to hear feedback on the live part of the experience. What are your thoughts on the balance between live help vs after-visit? Would something pre-visit be more helpful?

title.value: Show HN: We built a real-time desktop companion for patient's telehealth visits

story_text.value:
I've always been the person who types an emoji into a form just to see what happens. Most of the bugs I've reported are really about data that my code assumed would look a certain way.

So I built ChaosData. Give it a schema, and it generates realistic data with a few deliberate edge cases mixed in. Emojis where they shouldn't be, malformed strings, edge-case integers, etc.

  mysqldump --no-data shop | curl -s -X POST \
    "https://chaosdata.net/api/v1/quick-generate?rows=100&chaos=20" \
    -H "Accept: text/sql" --data-binary @- | mysql shop_test
Some tools generate realisitc data, and some generate chaotic data, but we'll do both (and respect your schema)!

There are lots of ways I could go from here, but I wanted to see if I could get some input first before I took it further.

I'd love any thoughts or feedback.

title.value: Show HN: ChaosData – Chaotic data that fits your schema
